practice.solution: 'Since' needs the perfect, and 'know' is a stative verb that does not take a continuous form. That leaves **have known**. 'Are knowing' and 'had been knowing' break the stative rule, and 'know' ignores since.
practice.shortcut: Stative verb + since -> present perfect simple.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

When we reached the platform, the train ___.
practice.solution: Two past events: the train left first and we reached later. The earlier one takes the past perfect: **had already left**. 'Has already left' clashes with the past 'reached'.
practice.shortcut: Earlier of two past events -> had + V3.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

No sooner ___ the principal entered the hall than the students stood up.
practice.solution: The frame is 'No sooner had + subject + V3 ... than + simple past': **had** entered. 'Did' would need the base form 'enter', 'has' clashes with 'stood', and 'was entered' is a wrong passive.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

If it ___ tomorrow, the match will be postponed.
practice.solution: Type-1 conditional: the if-clause takes the simple present (**rains**) and the main clause takes will. 'Will' never enters the if-clause; 'rained' and 'would rain' belong to type 2.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Had she left home earlier, she ___ the flight.
practice.solution: The inverted 'Had she left' is a type-3 (unreal past) condition, so the result takes **would have caught**. 'Would catch' is type 2, 'will catch' is type 1, and 'had caught' has no would.
practice.shortcut: Had + subject + V3 ... would have + V3.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The children enjoy ___ in the rain.
practice.solution: 'Enjoy' is followed by a gerund: enjoy **playing**. 'Enjoy to play' is the common slip; 'play' and 'to playing' are not possible after enjoy.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The committee decided ___ the event to December.
practice.solution: 'Decide' takes the infinitive: decided **to postpone**. 'Decided postponing' uses the gerund wrongly; the bare verb and 'to postponing' are ungrammatical here.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Neither of the two answers ___ correct.
practice.solution: 'Neither of + plural noun' takes a singular verb because neither (not one) is the head. So **is**. 'Are', 'were' and 'have been' agree with 'answers', the trap noun.
practice.shortcut: neither of / each of -> singular verb.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The number of applicants for the post ___ increased sharply this year.
practice.solution: 'The number of' is singular (one number), so **has** increased. 'A number of' would be plural — that is the distinction being tested. 'Are increased' and 'were increased' are wrong passives with the wrong number.
practice.shortcut: THE number -> singular; A number -> plural.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

No sooner had the rain stopped ___ the children ran out to play.
practice.solution: 'No sooner' pairs only with **than**. 'When' belongs to hardly or scarcely, 'then' is a time adverb, and 'that' is not a correlative.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The patient had scarcely reached the hospital ___ he lost consciousness.
practice.solution: 'Scarcely' (like hardly) pairs with **when**. 'Than' is the partner of no sooner, the mix-up the question is testing; 'then' and 'so' do not complete the frame.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

This is the house ___ roof was damaged in the storm.
practice.solution: The roof belongs to the house, which is possession, so **whose** is needed ('whose' is allowed for things). 'Which roof' would start a question, and 'who' and 'whom' refer to people.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The scientist to ___ the award was given belongs to Kerala.
practice.solution: After a preposition, the object form is required: to **whom**. 'To who' is ungrammatical, 'to which' refers to things, and 'whose' needs a following noun.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

He was exhausted, ___ he kept working till midnight.
practice.solution: Being exhausted and still working are in contrast, so the connector is **yet**. 'So' and 'therefore' would treat working late as a result of exhaustion, and 'because' would make exhaustion its cause.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The flight was cancelled ___ the dense fog over the airport.
practice.solution: Fog is the cause, and a noun phrase ('the dense fog') follows, so **because of** is needed. 'Because' needs a full clause, and 'although' and 'despite' express contrast, not cause.
practice.shortcut: Cause + noun -> because of / owing to.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The students decorated the classroom ___.
practice.solution: The students did it without help, which calls for the reflexive of 'they': **themselves**. 'Theirselves' and 'themself' are non-standard, and 'ourselves' does not match the subject.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The company has changed ___ logo after twenty years.
practice.solution: The possessive of 'it' is **its**, with no apostrophe. 'It's' means 'it is' ('it is logo' makes no sense), 'its'' is not a word, and 'it' is not possessive.
practice.shortcut: Expand it's -> it is; if nonsense, use its.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ being the favourites, the team lost in the first round.
practice.solution: A gerund phrase ('being the favourites') follows the blank, so the contrast word must take a noun or gerund: **Despite**. 'Although' and 'though' need a full clause ('Although they were the favourites'), and 'however' cannot introduce a phrase.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ he had a fracture in his wrist, he completed the exam.
practice.solution: A full clause follows ('he had a fracture'), and the sense is contrast, so **Even though** fits. 'Despite' and 'In spite of' need a noun phrase ('despite the fracture'), and 'Owing to' expresses cause.
practice.shortcut: Clause after the blank -> although / even though.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

I ___ you to check the timetable before leaving.
practice.solution: The slot comes after the subject 'I' and takes an object, so a verb is needed: **advise**. 'Advice' is the noun (and is uncountable, so 'advices' is wrong), and 'adviser' is a person.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

There is no ___ that the accused was present at the scene.
practice.solution: After 'no' a noun is needed: **proof**. 'Prove' and 'proves' are verb forms, and 'proven' is a participle.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Tighten the screw; it has come ___.
practice.solution: A screw that is not tight is **loose**, and 'come loose' is the phrase. 'Lose' is a verb meaning misplace, 'loss' is a noun, and 'lost' means misplaced.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Lack of sleep can seriously ___ a student's concentration.
practice.solution: The sense is influence, and the slot follows 'can', so the verb **affect** is needed. 'Effect' as a verb means bring about, which does not fit here; 'affection' and 'effective' are the wrong parts of speech.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The ___ of the school addressed the students at the morning assembly.
practice.solution: The head of a school is the **principal**. 'Principle' means a rule or belief, 'principality' is a state ruled by a prince, and 'principled' is an adjective.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The car remained ___ at the signal even after the light turned green.
practice.solution: Not moving = **stationary**. 'Stationery' means writing materials, a 'stationer' sells them, and 'station' is a noun that cannot describe the car here.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The film board ___ two violent scenes before granting the certificate.
practice.solution: Cutting content from a film is **censoring** it. 'Censured' means formally rebuked, which applies to people and conduct, not to scenes; 'sensored' is not a word, and 'sensed' means perceived.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The poem contains an ___ to an episode from the Mahabharata.
practice.solution: An indirect reference is an **allusion**, and 'allusion to' is the standard pattern. 'Illusion' is a false appearance, 'elusion' means escape, and 'delusion' is a false belief — none is a reference.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ the teachers ___ the principal was informed about the inspection.
practice.solution: The verb is singular ('was'), which rules out 'Both ... and' (that needs 'were'). With **Neither ... nor**, the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the principal', which is singular, so 'was' fits. 'Neither ... or' and 'Either ... nor' mix partners that never go together.
practice.shortcut: Singular verb + correct partners -> neither ... nor.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The new policy will benefit ___ farmers ___ small traders.
practice.solution: Only **not only ... but also** is a correct pair here. 'Neither ... or', 'either ... nor' and 'both ... or' each mix partners from different pairs.
practice.shortcut: Check that the partners match first.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ you finish the project on time ___ you forfeit the bonus.
practice.solution: The sentence offers two alternatives — finish on time, or lose the bonus — so **Either ... or** fits. 'Neither ... nor' before two clauses would need inversion and would deny both. 'Both ... and' makes nonsense of the choice, and 'Whether ... nor' is not a pair.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

After two days at sea, the missing fishermen returned home ___ and ___.
practice.solution: Returning unharmed is returning **safe and sound**. 'Null and void' means legally invalid, 'part and parcel' means essential, and 'odds and ends' means small leftover items.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ and ___, every candidate must carry a valid photo identity card.
practice.solution: The sentence opens with the most important instruction, so the idiom is **First and foremost**. The other pairs are real idioms, but none can introduce a priority.
practice.shortcut: Most important point = first and foremost.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The office remains open ___ 9 a.m. ___ 5 p.m.
practice.solution: A start-to-end range takes **from ... to**. 'From ... and' and 'between ... to' mix partners, and 'since' marks a starting point up to now, not a daily range.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The border dispute ___ India ___ its neighbour was settled through talks.
practice.solution: Two parties take **between ... and**. 'Among' is for three or more, 'between ... with' mixes partners, and 'from ... to' marks a range, not a dispute between two sides.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ had he left the house ___ it began to pour.
practice.solution: The fixed frames are 'Hardly ... when' and 'No sooner ... than'. Only **Hardly ... when** keeps its true partner; the other three cross the pairs.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ had the result been declared ___ the students started celebrating.
practice.solution: Only **No sooner ... than** is a matched pair. 'No sooner ... when' and 'Hardly ... than' cross the two frames, and 'then' is never a correlative partner.
practice.shortcut: Match the partners; then is always a decoy.
